news.title: Trump cancels Iran attack, calls for immediate deal, claims Israel supporting commitment
news.text: US President Donald Trump called for an immediate deal with Iran in a Truth Social post on Saturday night, claiming to have called off a massive attack against the country and to have Israel's support in his commitment."The USA is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II," Trump claimed. "Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to."Trump announced that the deal would have to include the complete opening of the Strait of Hormuz, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat."Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump wrote.Earlier on Saturday, two Israeli sources told The Jerusalem Post that Israel had raised the alert and readiness amid assessments that US President Donald Trump was close to deciding to resume military strikes against Iran, potentially on an even larger scale.Israeli officials told the Post that “we are on high alert and awaiting the president's final decision.”This is a developing story.

news.title: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asks Trump to reconsider large strikes on Iran - report
news.text: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked US President Donald Trump to reconsider potential large military strikes on Iran during a phone call on Saturday, Axios reported on Sunday.The report cited two United States officials, one of whom told Axios that "the Saudis expressed concern and asked for clarity about the plan of action." Axios further cited sources with knowledge of the call between the two world leaders, who said that Salman asked Trump to de-escalate the situation instead of launching large strikes.According to the report, the Saudis are concerned that the strikes could result in an unprecedented regional escalation.Axios reached out to the Saudi Embassy in Washington and the White House, both of which declined to comment.The report comes as two Israeli sources told The Jerusalem Post that Israel has raised its alert and readiness for a potential resumption of large US strikes on Iran.Countries across region ask Trump to avoid large strikesOther countries in the region have also asked Trump to avoid escalating the situation, including Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, and Pakistan, according to the report.According to Axios, indirect talks on Saturday between the US and Iran have resulted in some progress, though no agreement has been reached.Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

news.title: Herzog accuses Mamdani of spreading 'blasphemy,' antisemitism, after stabbing attack
news.text: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is spreading "blasphemy," as well as antisemitism, President Isaac Herzog told Fox News in an interview published on Saturday."Mamdani does not respect my nation's right for self-determination," Herzog accused the mayor. "He's basically spreading blasphemy, hate, antisemitic rhetoric. He should understand that he's risking his own citizens. He's risking their safety, well-being and life."Herzog referenced a recent stabbing which occurred in New York against two men, one of whom was Jewish, blaming Mamdani's rhetoric for the violence."I think New York will continue way after Mamdani, and I hope he won't create any irreversible damage, and I hope the citizens of New York will be as safe as was promised to them," Herzog stated.He also condemned former International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutor Karim Khan, accusing him of having attempted to use the arrest warrants issued against various Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as a distraction from the sexual harassment allegations against him.Khan, Herzog claimed, had been ready to visit Israel and meet with Israeli officials, including Herzog himself, when the trip was suddenly called off amid his announcement of the arrest warrants."That case has to be dropped, and the ICC should revert it completely, and not fall into the trap of hate and lies that Karim Khan presented simply to cover for himself," Herzog demanded.US, Israel bonded by spiritual values, Herzog claimsHerzog also said there was something "Biblical and prophetic" in how the United States and Israel worked together, citing US President Donald Trump's support for Israel, and called for bipartisan "friendship and support" between the two countries."We both drink from the fountain of the Bible," he said. "We both drink from this set of values which was commanded to all of us by these historic, spiritual books given to us by the Almighty."He blamed much of the current tension between Israel and the younger generation of Americans on social media, saying that it was "very easy to smear Israel on TikTok, but that doesn't say the real truth."Israel, Herzog defended, was a democracy with a wide variety of opinions within its political parties, "from Palestinian-oriented parties, to extreme right-wing, even fascist, on the verge of fascism parties," he explained.Iran a threat to stability due to ideology, Herzog saysThe president also discussed the war with Iran, saying that the Iranian regime was a threat to stability across the region."Think about it, they take their people's food and money and spend it on terror all over the world. It's a given fact," he said. "You ask yourself, why?"According to Herzog, the reason for Iran's relentless pursuit of global terror activity is ideology."The ideology does not accommodate any other religion or moderate Islam, for that matter. That is why it is so dangerous," he explained. "You see it in their missile program, you see it in Hormuz, you see it in the nuclear desire, you see it in the butchering of tens of thousands of its citizens... Look how much suffering. So many American citizens were killed by this regime."

news.title: Trump calls off planned weekend strikes on new Iran targets as he hints at shock deal to REOPEN Strait of Hormuz
news.text:

The president said on Truth Social on Saturday evening that although he remains 'locked and loaded' to launch an attack, he halted the strikes in hopes of reaching a peace deal.

'This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat. 

'Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL. 

'The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE. Thank you for your attention to this matter!

news.title: Trump Says US 'Locked And Loaded' Against Iran, Agrees To Cancel Attack Over Hormuz Deal
news.text: US President Donald Trump said the United States was "locked and loaded" and ready to launch military action against Iran "at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II," but announced he had agreed to cancel the planned attack after Iran and other Middle Eastern countries requested a hold-off, citing an agreement to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end Tehran's nuclear threat. "The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II. Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to. This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat. Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump posted on his social media platform, Truth Social. "The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE. Thank you for your attention to this matter!" he added.
news.summary: Trump said the US was "locked and loaded" for attack against Iran but agreed to cancel it after Iran and regional countries sought a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end its nuclear threat.
news.author: Apoorva Shukla

news.title: A look at the feminist 4B movement
news.text: p>For the tradwives (traditional wives) of the internet, the 4B movement might be the stuff nightmares are made of. While the tradwives have been busy trying to undo everything the feminists have achieved over centuries, a decade-old movement brewing in South Korea, is asking for a radical change. Built on not only dismantling patriarchy but also taking it a step further by boycotting men, the movement is gaining momentum worldwide..Although South Korea is known to be a modern economy, the gender climate has been punctuated with violence, online hate speech against women, rigid beauty standards, workplace harassment, and digital sex crimes. The 4B movement, which emerged as a response to this in the mid-2010s, has now sparked interest beyond South Korea..Beyond the wellness industry: Holding space, for self and beyond.The “B” comes from the Korean word bi, which means “no”. The movement firmly sits on four refusals: bihon (no marriage), bichulsan (no childbirth), biyeonae (no dating men) and bisekseu (no sex with a man). Since its initial days, women have emphasised that the movement is rooted in autonomy and rejection of traditional expectations such as heterosexual marriage, motherhood, and any kind of intimacy with men. Interestingly, in 2024, after Donald Trump’s re-election as president, women in the United States turned to this movement as a way of defiance, with Google searches for “4B” increasing by 450%. Meanwhile, women in China, inspired by 4B, opted for 6B4T, which expands it further by rejecting beauty consumerism, emotional labour for men as well as restrictive beauty standards, religion, otaku subcultures (obsession with anime, manga, and video games) and idol worship. While the 4B movement has sparked online conversations in India, it’s yet to spark a shared rebellion..(Curated by Aisiri Amin).(Decoded demystifies gender concepts and breaks them down into easy-to-understand language.)</p

news.title: Trump faces ethics storm for ‘pimping’ fast access to his Truth Social posts
news.text:
US President Donald Trump knows the world hangs on his every word. Now he wants you to pay for it.
The social media posts of the world’s most powerful man went on sale on Saturday, when his Truth Social business began offering sneak peeks of them to Wall Street traders willing to pay up. The move raises the prospect of big profits for Trump’s company and big questions about insider trading and using public office for private gain.
Similar fast speed feeds are sold by other social media firms and media providers, but Truth Social does not just distribute the news; it makes it, regularly rattling markets as Trump posts policy changes on everything from war to central bank leadership to tariffs.
If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time
Irene Aldridge, head of Able Alpha Trading
“If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time,” said Irene Aldridge, head of Able Alpha Trading, which does not plan to buy the service. “We have a president of the United States who has the front seat to all the action, who makes all the decisions, and he’s disclosing this ahead of time to a select group.”
Asked about the propriety of the new service and whether White House lawyers had vetted it, Trump’s press office declined to comment, referring questions to Truth Social’s publicly traded parent.
That company, Trump Media & Technology, issued a statement blasting Democratic critics for mischaracterising the service “out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and non-public information – or, quite possibly, both”.

A prolific poster, Trump has sent stocks, bonds and currencies soaring and plunging with his online musings and threats. That presents opportunities for so-called high-frequency traders that specialise in buying and selling within milliseconds, exploiting tiny, fleeting differences in prices.
Last month alone, Trump threatened on Truth Social to slap higher tariffs on Canada, kill a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia and widen the Iran war. With advanced knowledge, traders betting on a plunge in the Canadian dollar, a drop in nuclear energy stocks and a jump in oil futures could have raked in big profits.
“For the big guys, it’s going to be something they need,” said Joe Saluzzi, co-founder of Themis Trading, who estimates about 100 of high frequency firms might be willing to pay for the service. “It’s market-moving information.”
Dubbed Truth API, the service comes as these firms are spending more on feeds and servers that bypass slower internet connections with direct lines to news and data sources.
The chance for profits is greater than ever thanks to artificial intelligence’s ability to read posts and articles more accurately for market-making changes and Trump’s penchant for making news online.

Traders profit when prices jump up and down and, with his taste for cliffhangers, threats and policy reversals, America’s first reality-TV president provides plenty of potentially market-moving content.
The reversals are especially profitable, allowing traders to win both ways – jumping ahead of stocks moving up or down to a post threatening something, then cashing out within thousands of a second, then betting the other way.
In addition to Trump, the service will include posts from other “high ranking” Truth Social contributors, including possibly his two oldest sons, Donald Jnr and Eric, who along with the father are heavily followed by users.
‘Real mess’
Truth Social has said that the information will be released to the traders and the general public at the same time, so there really is not an issue of fairness. But Themis Trading’s Saluzzi, a critic of high-speed trading, says that is a red herring because when the posts are received, not when they are released, is what matters.
“Somebody who buys the info and has a system built to process it will be able to act quicker than you and me,” said Saluzzi, adding in reference to everyday, small stock buyers, “The loser is always the retail investor.”
Aside from policy scoops, another reason to sign up has emerged in recent months: Trump is posting more about publicly traded companies, praising ones he likes in a way that sets off buying frenzies.
“The pimping of specific companies – obviously Wall Street would like to know that before other people,” said Dylan Hedler-Gaudette, a federal ethics rule expert at the watchdog Project on Government Oversight. “It’s a real mess.”

A prolific poster, Trump has sent stocks, bonds and currencies soaring and plunging with his online musings and threats. That presents opportunities for so-called high-frequency traders that specialise in buying and selling within milliseconds, exploiting tiny, fleeting differences in prices.
Asked for comment, none of the half-dozen most well-known high-speed traders such as Citadel Securities and XTX Markets replied. If just three sign up for the US$100,000 a month fee, that would double revenue at Trump Media, which reported taking in US$3.7 million last year.
The company can use their business. Stock in the Truth Social parent has plunged 75 per cent since Trump took office last year, as the company keeps reporting hundreds of millions in losses despite the president’s help driving traffic to its site by posting major decisions there.
In fact, the president breaks news on Truth Social so often that the White House press office will copy his posts into an email when responding to questions from the media seeking details on policies. If his posts are not available yet, journalists are sometimes told: “Wait for the Truth.”
Another problem for Truth Social is looming if the Democrats take control of Congress and launch investigations, as vowed by Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren in a statement on Friday specifically attacking the new service: “We will haul in those responsible for this open corruption to answer to the American people.”
If the losses keep mounting for the company, though, some predict the president will push things further, using the platform even more for policy announcements.
“That’s absolutely going to happen,” warned Craig Holman, a lobbyist for the good government group Public Citizen. “Trump knows how to sell products.”

news.title: 'Be Ready To Leave': US Warns Americans Across Middle East As Iran Tensions Escalate
news.text: The United States has issued a fresh security advisory for Americans across the Middle East, warning of escalating regional tensions linked to the ongoing conflict with Iran and urging citizens to be prepared for potential evacuations, flight cancellations and sudden travel disruptions. The advisory comes as US President Donald Trump threatened further military strikes on Iran, while fresh security incidents were reported in Kuwait, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gaza Strip, signalling that the conflict continues to widen. In its latest alert, the US State Department advised American citizens currently in the Middle East to “exercise caution and heightened vigilance" and remain prepared for deteriorating security conditions. Americans in the region were urged to consider departing or be ready to leave should the situation escalate further. The advisory warned that commercial flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures and other travel disruptions remain possible, adding that several airlines have postponed the resumption of normal flight schedules while others have cancelled routes across the region. The State Department also advised Americans travelling to or from the Middle East to closely monitor airport and airline operations before making travel plans. US Warns Of Possible Attacks On American Interests Worldwide The security alert extended beyond the Middle East, warning that Iran and groups aligned with Tehran could target American diplomatic facilities, businesses and institutions across the world. The State Department noted that US diplomatic missions, including those outside the Middle East, have already been targeted in recent months. “Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions," the advisory said. The warning applies to Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Americans outside the Middle East were also urged to “seriously reconsider travel to and through the region" until tensions ease. Trump Threatens More Strikes On Iran The advisory was issued hours after Trump warned that the United States was prepared to continue military action against Iran. According to the Associated Press (AP), Trump told reporters during a Cabinet meeting at the Camp David presidential retreat that the US would continue striking Iran if necessary. “We just want to win," Trump said, adding that the United States would hit Iran “very hard" until it “can’t take it anymore," AP reported. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt later accused Tehran of violating an earlier truce understanding with Washington. According to AP, Leavitt alleged that Iran had signed a memorandum of understanding with the US but later “broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers." “President Trump is not going to stand by and allow this terrorist behaviour to occur. Iran will continue to pay until they come to the table in what President Trump deems a meaningful way," she said, according to AP. Conflict Expands Across Gulf And Gaza The latest US advisory comes amid fresh violence across multiple fronts in the Middle East. According to AP, Kuwait said on Saturday that its military responded to a new round of Iranian drone attacks targeting several vital facilities, including a government building in the country’s north. Authorities said no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, the British Navy reported two separate maritime security incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most strategically important shipping routes. AP reported that an unidentified projectile struck a tanker near Oman, damaging its engine room, while another explosion occurred close to a separate vessel near Khasab. No casualties were reported in either incident. Separately, satellite images reviewed by AP showed crude oil leaking from a sanctioned tanker grounded off the coast of Oman near a protected marine area. The Strait of Hormuz has remained a major flashpoint throughout the conflict, with AP reporting that Iran has repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to transit the strategic waterway without its authorisation. Israeli Strikes Continue Despite Hamas Disarmament Announcement The conflict also intensified in Gaza despite a potential diplomatic breakthrough. According to AP, Hamas confirmed on Friday that it had agreed to disarm under a US-brokered ceasefire framework announced last October. The proposed agreement calls for Hamas to surrender its weapons, transfer governing authority to an independent Palestinian administration, while Israeli forces would withdraw and an International Stabilisation Force would be deployed. However, despite the announcement, Israeli forces launched heavy overnight strikes across central and northern Gaza. AP reported that at least four people were killed and dozens injured in the attacks, while Israel’s military said it struck Hamas targets and destroyed five weapons storage facilities. Reacting to the proposed agreement, Israeli far-right lawmaker Itamar Ben-Gvir described the deal as “unacceptable" and said military operations should continue, according to AP. Egypt, which has played a key mediating role in ceasefire negotiations, welcomed what it described as Hamas’ “positive response" to the phased peace proposal, AP reported. Regional Security Concerns Continue To Grow The latest developments highlight growing fears that the conflict could spread further beyond Iran and Israel. In addition to the fighting in Gaza and rising tensions in the Gulf, AP reported that Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed they forced several Saudi ships to reroute away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait after announcing a blockade on Saudi shipping. In southern Lebanon, Israeli forces also destroyed an underground tunnel network beneath the historic Beaufort Castle, claiming it had served as a Hezbollah command centre. Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun criticised the operation, saying it sent “negative messages" ahead of planned negotiations between Israel and Lebanon in Rome, AP reported.
news.summary: The US has issued a new security advisory for Americans in the Middle East due to rising tensions linked to Iran, cautioning citizens to be prepared for possible evacuations and travel disruptions.
news.author: Megha Rawat

news.title: Capital One shuts Trump Organization's accounts after anti-money laundering probe
news.text:
ANIUS President Donald Trump

SAN FRANCISCO - Capital One Financial hit back on Friday against a lawsuit over its decision to close the Trump Organization's bank accounts years ago, stating that it did so after a review by anti-money laundering experts.The disclosure marks the first time a bank ‌has formally tied money ⁠laundering concerns ⁠to U.S. President Donald Trump's family business. Capital One is seeking to dismiss the case by casting doubt on claims of illegally debanking - ​or denying services on religious or political grounds - the Trump Organization.The Trump Organization and Capital One did not immediately respond to requests ​for comment.Capital One has never accused the Trump Organization of illegal money laundering. But Friday's filing argues that "documents and Plaintiffs' own allegations make clear that Capital One closed Plaintiffs' accounts for anti-money laundering ("AML") reasons. The closures were the ​result of months of analysis and a careful review by Capital One's ⁠AML team in ‌accordance with bank policies and regulatory guidance."Capital One gave notice of its plans to close more than 300 Trump-affiliated bank accounts in March 2021. The Trump Organization and Eric Trump, the ⁠president's son, filed a lawsuit in March 2025 in a Florida federal court, alleging the accounts were closed because of Capital One's "woke" beliefs and its desire to benefit from the political mood after the January 6, 2021 riot at the U.S. Capitol.Live EventsYou Might Also Like:Trump stands to profit off US policy announcements by selling fast access to his social media posts'MISGUIDED' ALLEGATIONS: CAPITAL ONEThe federal court in Miami has tossed two complaints in the Capital One case, but gave the plaintiffs opportunities each time to submit an amended complaint. Capital One said that the latest version, filed in July, "suffers from the same fundamental flaws as their prior two pleadings."Capital One said in Friday's filing that the Trump Organization's allegations of political ‌pretext were "misguided" and "based on cherry-picked quotations unsupported by the full context" of documents submitted to the court."The transaction patterns identified by Capital One are among the types of activity flagged by ​federal banking guidance," the ​filing said.Since the start of ⁠Trump's second term, his administration has put pressure on some large banks, echoing conservative complaints that the institutions are deliberately targeting the political right. Trump signed an executive order in August 2025 barring discriminatory debanking.In January, Trump filed a ​suit against JPMorgan Chase on the same grounds, underscoring the fraught policy environment Wall Street is navigating during the president's second term.In 2019, during his first term, Trump sued Capital One and Deutsche Bank in an attempt to prevent them from sharing financial records with Congress as part of a probe led by Democratic lawmakers. news.title: Vincent Pastore, who played mob enforcer on 'The Sopranos,' dies at 80
news.text: Veteran American actor Vincent Pastore, widely recognised for his portrayal of mob enforcer-turned-FBI informant Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero in HBO's landmark series "The Sopranos," has died at the age of 80, according to a report by news agency AFP that cited a statement from his manager.Actor Found Dead At His Home In The BronxThe actor's manager, Robert Attermann, confirmed the news of his death to AFP on Saturday, though he did not disclose details surrounding the circumstances. Separately, Hollywood entertainment outlet Deadline reported that Pastore, a native of New York, was found dead at his home in The Bronx on Saturday.From The US Navy To A Career In HollywoodBorn on July 14, 1946, Pastore's journey to Hollywood began far from the film sets he would later become known for. He served in the United States Navy during the Vietnam War before going on to complete a university degree in drama, laying the foundation for what would become a decades-long acting career.Over the years, Pastore carved out a niche playing archetypal New York gangster characters, a persona he brought to life across several notable film projects. He appeared in Martin Scorsese's celebrated 1990 crime drama "Goodfellas," and also featured in Brian De Palma's 1993 film "Carlito's Way," both of which further cemented his association with mob-themed storytelling on screen.However, it was his role as "Big Pussy" in "The Sopranos" that became the defining moment of his career. In the show, Pastore played a close aide to lead character Tony Soprano, portrayed by the late James Gandolfini, before his character's storyline took a dramatic turn when he was revealed to be secretly informing the FBI.That storyline culminated in what remains one of the most talked-about moments in the Emmy-winning series' run — his character's murder at the end of the show's second season. In the scene, Pastore's character utters the now-famous line, "Not in the face, ok?" moments before he is shot multiple times at close range by Tony Soprano and two other associates, a sequence that has continued to be referenced by fans of the show years after it first aired.Beyond his time on "The Sopranos," Pastore built a fairly expansive career across television and film. He made guest appearances on several popular American television series, including "Law and Order" and "The Practice." He also lent his voice to the animated film "Shark Tale," adding an animated feature to his otherwise largely live-action filmography.In addition to his acting credits, Pastore also became a familiar face on American reality television, appearing on shows such as "The Celebrity Apprentice" during the period when Donald Trump, now the sitting US President, was still hosting the programme.Paying tribute to the actor, his longtime manager Robert Attermann noted that he had represented Pastore for more than three decades, long before "The Sopranos" turned him into a household name. In his statement, Attermann said, "To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable 'Big Pussy'," while adding that those who knew him personally saw a far more layered individual beyond the character that made him famous.Attermann further reflected on Pastore's dedication to his craft, describing him as someone who genuinely loved being an actor and remained deeply passionate about the profession throughout his career. He also spoke about Pastore's approach toward younger actors in the industry, noting that he was consistently encouraging, respectful and generous with his time, often going out of his way to offer guidance and support to those newer to the field whenever the opportunity arose.Pastore's death marks the loss of yet another prominent name associated with "The Sopranos," a series that continues to hold a significant place in television history and remains popular among audiences globally, including a considerable fan base in India that has followed the show through streaming platforms over the years.
news.author: Anjali Thakur

news.title: Google rolls back new satellite image AI tool after backlash
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Google rolled back on July 31 a new feature allowing Google Earth users to generate AI visualisations on top of the service's satellite imagery, following a furious backlash from researchers and open-source intelligence experts about the potential for disinformation.

"We've seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however, we've also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies," a Google spokesperson said in a statement to AFP. "So we're rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails."

"We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world," the statement added.

The "create image" tool, unveiled on July 30, had integrated Google's Nano Banana 2 image-generation technology into Google Earth, letting users zoom into locations and build pictures in seconds based on the program's satellite, aerial and 3D-mapping data.

Google had described it as a way to "visualise history, create real estate plans and more."

But disinformation researchers warned that it could enable bad actors to misuse Google Earth – a key resource for fact-checking and verification – to create realistic geospatial fakes.

"Google spent 20 years building the reference the world checks against," digital investigations expert Henk Van Ess wrote in one widely shared post on Substack. "Today it added a button that makes things up."

Brady Africk, a research analyst at the American Enterprise Institute specialising in satellite imagery analysis, told AFP the Google Earth update would have made it "easier to generate convincing fake satellite imagery that can spread quickly online and mislead the public."

Such fakes "erode public trust in satellite imagery, and make the jobs of journalists and researchers more difficult," he said.

'Irrevocably damaged overnight'

As the critiques piled up, Google had said on X that the images created with the feature included SynthID digital watermarks, invisible markers embedded in media generated using the company's artificial intelligence (AI) tools.

"We take misinformation seriously," the company wrote, linking to an AI policy that instructs users against "misinformation, misrepresentation or misleading activities."

AFP's tests of the feature on July 31 were able to fabricate satellite images that could have had serious global consequences: an explosion in Paris, a nuclear site in Iran, a bomb crater in Russia and an Islamic State group training ground in Syria.

The tool also fulfilled prompts to visualise other fake scenes, including floods across Bangladesh, a migrant caravan camped at the US-Mexico border and a suspicious warehouse holding vans in Georgia – one of several states US President Donald Trump has falsely accused of widespread election fraud.

The "create image" button no longer appeared within Google Earth after Google paused its use.

Similar fakes have previously had real-world impacts. In 2023, an AI image depicting an explosion at the Pentagon briefly rattled the markets.

Early in the US war with Iran, an AI-altered satellite image depicting a destroyed US military base garnered millions of views across platforms.

Among the groups that called for Google to reverse its decision was the London-based Centre for Information Resilience, whose executive director Ross Burley told AFP the feature was "irresponsible."

"Trust in satellite imagery has taken decades to build and could be irrevocably damaged overnight," Burley said.

GeoConfirmed, a volunteer-driven open-source intelligence project that verifies visuals from conflicts around the globe, had also urged Google to reconsider.

"We are already observing individuals exploiting the new Google Earth web tool to make military positions, relabel buildings as schools, and experiment with manipulating the information environment," the group wrote on X, before Google announced it was rolling back the feature.

"The primary, and perhaps only, practical use of this tool appears to be the creation and dissemination of mis- and disinformation." – AFP
news.author: Bill McCarthy

news.title: Michael Goodwin: Fauci’s refusal to answer questions at Senate hearing reveals important truth

news.title: Family of hero teen lifeguard finalizing plans for White House visit after Trump praised miraculous beach rescue
news.text:
California’s teenage lifeguard hero could soon be headed to the White House.

The family of 16-year-old Ryder Williams has been contacted by President Donald Trump’s staff after the commander-in-chief vowed to honor the rookie rescuer who saved a drowning 10-year-old boy from pounding surf.

“The White House has contacted us but there’s been no official date or time,” Ryder’s father, retired firefighter Shane Williams, 54, told The California Post on Saturday.

Trump announced the invitation after video of Ryder’s dramatic rescue at Seabright Beach went viral, saying he plans to welcome the teen and his family to Washington, DC, and personally present him with a high civilian honor for his heroism.

Shane said the whirlwind of attention has been overwhelming, but the family is now focused on returning to everyday life as Ryder prepares for his first day of school on Aug. 6.

“We just want to get back to normal life and let him start high school and start playing water polo,” he said.

The proud father also welcomed the president’s recognition of his son.“I would love to take my son there and I think he deserves that.”

Shane said Ryder is not doing interviews outside those arranged through California State Parks. He added that he couldn’t remember which White House staffer had called because his phone had been “blowing up.”

Shane declined to discuss when the family might travel to Washington and would not say whether Ryder plans to reunite with 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai, saying any updates would come through California State Parks.

Ryder became an overnight hero on July 25 after an 8-to-10-foot sneaker wave dragged Nathaniel, of Dallas, into deep water at Seabright Beach.

The rookie lifeguard battled heavy surf for about two minutes to reach the boy after he blacked out in the water.Fellow lifeguard Aaron Bohnen swam out to help, and together they brought Nathaniel safely to shore, where he was revived. 

The boy is expected to make a full recovery.

The rescue unfolded during a chaotic day that saw Santa Cruz district lifeguards perform 34 rescues.

Nathaniel’s father, Sumit Rai, previously told The Post he was “so grateful” to Ryder for saving his son’s life.

news.title: A new arms race? How Trump's Saudi nuclear deal could destabilise Middle East
news.text: As Donald Trump continues his stop-start campaign to dismantle Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, and now also to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, history suggests that it was one of his predecessors, president Dwight D. Eisenhower, who helped lay the foundation for Tehran’s nuclear programme. When the United States signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Iran in 1957, it became the fourth country in the Middle East, after Turkey, Lebanon and Israel, to secure such a deal. Under Eisenhower’s ‘Atoms for Peace’ programme, the US supplied technical assistance, research equipment, a reactor and enriched uranium fuel. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology even established a graduate programme that trained Iranian nuclear engineers. Saudi Arabia, now among America's closest allies, had to wait nearly 70 years for a nuclear deal, one that could yet prove to be no agreement at all. Trump's decision to offer Riyadh a sweeping civil nuclear deal stunned many observers, especially as it came in the middle of the war against Iran. The proposal appeared unusually generous, close to capabilities such as domestic uranium enrichment that Washington insists Iran should not possess. Then, within 24 hours, Trump changed course. He declared that the agreement would proceed only if Saudi Arabia joined the Abraham Accords and recognised Israel, a condition Riyadh is never likely to accept. The episode highlighted a nuclear policy that shifts according to who Trump sees as a friend and who he chooses to confront. The deal was not simply about helping Saudi Arabia diversify its energy mix. Trump clearly saw an opportunity to revive the American nuclear industry that has struggled for decades. The deal could attract contracts worth billions of dollars, with Westinghouse expected to supply AP1000 reactors to the kingdom. Although the US still operates more nuclear reactors than any other country, it has completed only a handful of new reactors since the 1990s, while China has expanded its fleet at remarkable speed. And the Saudi deal was supposed to change all that. "The administration has been pitching this agreement as a business proposition that will establish a legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar nuclear energy partnership with the kingdom," writes Jane Darby Menton of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Strategic concerns reinforced the commercial logic. Washington feared that refusing Saudi Arabia access to advanced nuclear technology would simply push Riyadh towards Russia or China. The White House also saw the agreement as a way of repairing strains in a relationship unsettled by the fallout from the Iran war and restoring the traditional closeness that has long characterised US-Saudi ties. Yet Trump’s triumph lasted barely a day. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman had barely finished signing the agreement on July 22 before Trump announced that it would be conditional. The reversal appeared to be driven less by strategic calculation than by political pressure. Fox News, Trump's preferred television network, and a critical Wall Street Journal editorial board questioned why Riyadh had received such generous terms—minimal international oversight, permission for enrichment—without offering the diplomatic recognition of Israel that Washington had sought under former president Joe Biden. Trump, reportedly upset with the Biden reference and also because Wright had announced the agreement without his final approval, responded in typically transactional fashion by attaching a new condition, hoping to blunt further criticism. The move caught Saudi officials, and even American negotiators, by surprise. Yet the larger story lies not in the chaos surrounding the agreement, but in its substance. For critics, the Saudi deal exposed the double standards at the heart of Washington’s nuclear diplomacy. Even as the US targets the Iranian nuclear programme, the agreement with Riyadh opens the door to uranium enrichment on Saudi soil. The agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency's additional protocol, the inspection mechanism that allows instant access to ensure that nuclear material is not diverted for military purposes. That represents a significant departure from previous American policy. When Washington concluded its civil nuclear agreement with the United Arab Emirates in 2009, it was hailed as the non-proliferation ‘gold standard’ because Abu Dhabi permanently renounced uranium enrichment and accepted comprehensive IAEA safeguards. US officials have attempted to explain the contradiction away by arguing that any Saudi enrichment would occur within an American-operated "black box". Experts, however, dismiss the concept as unrealistic. No technical arrangement can ultimately prevent a sovereign state from exercising control over nuclear material located within its own territory. Riccardo Alcaro, research coordinator at the Istituto Affari Internazionali in Rome, writes that the Saudi agreement creates a troubling precedent by allowing verification standards to be negotiated bilaterally instead of relying on internationally accepted norms. Washington, in effect, appears willing to adjust the rules according to the identity of its negotiating partner. The implications extend far beyond one bilateral agreement. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has repeatedly stated that Saudi Arabia will seek a nuclear weapon if Iran acquires one. By granting Riyadh the building blocks of a complete nuclear fuel cycle without the safeguards imposed on the UAE, Washington risks accelerating precisely the regional nuclear competition it claims to oppose. Israel, whose undeclared nuclear monopoly has long been the backbone of its strategic position, has watched these developments with growing concern. More broadly, a lower non-proliferation threshold for Saudi Arabia could encourage Russia and China to offer similarly flexible arrangements to their partners, weakening the international non-proliferation regime. The special deal offered to Saudi Arabia could also influence any peace deal to end the Iran war. Although US and Israeli strikes have inflicted significant damage on Iran's nuclear facilities, experts broadly agree there is no convincing evidence that the country's nuclear infrastructure has been permanently dismantled. "Any prospect for lasting peace therefore depends on a new nuclear agreement between Washington and Tehran. If a renewed ceasefire were to lead to a negotiation, Iran would consider the terms of the Saudi deal as the baseline," explains Alcaro. Tehran would have every reason to reject restrictions that are not applied consistently to others, especially in the region. Despite Trump's repeated claims to have mastered the art of the deal, nuclear diplomacy has exposed the limits of his negotiating style. His first attempt with Iran, led largely by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, both real estate developers with no background in nuclear diplomacy, ended in the ongoing unpopular war. His Saudi initiative may yet become another failed negotiation. The contrast with the Obama administration's approach could hardly be sharper. The negotiations in Switzerland that produced the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) relied not only on hard-nosed diplomacy but also on personal touch. When Ali Akbar Salehi, the MIT-trained head of Iran's Atomic Energy Organisation, was tapped to assist foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, the Obama administration quietly brought energy secretary Ernest Moniz, himself an MIT graduate and nuclear physicist, into the American negotiating team. When Salehi was finishing his thesis on fast-neutron reactors at MIT in 1977, Moniz was a young nuclear scientist pursuing tenure there. The shared background proved invaluable as they played central roles in resolving some of the negotiations' most technically complex issues. During one marathon session in Lausanne, news came that Salehi's daughter gave birth to a son. Moniz surprised his Iranian counterpart with baby gifts from the official MIT gift shop. Salehi later returned from Tehran with traditional Iranian presents for Moniz's family. Looking back, the JCPOA was about as good a nuclear deal as the US was ever going to get.

news.title: Saudi Crown Prince Urges Trump Not To Escalate Iran War As U.S. Leader Weighs New Strikes: AP Source
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, in a phone call with President Donald Trump on Saturday raised concerns about the U.S. potentially escalating the conflict with Iran, according to a person familiar with the leaders’ discussion.

The discussion, which was first reported on by Axios, comes as Trump weighs whether to carry out new strikes on Iran.

The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call but not authorized to comment publicly, are concerned that if the U.S. targets Iran’s energy infrastructure or carries out massive strikes on other key infrastructure that Tehran could respond by carrying out attacks on the kingdom’s and other Gulf countries’ energy infrastructure.

The crown prince during Saturday’s call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he’s weighing to take against Iran, the person said.

The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Saturday’s call.

news.title: Trump stands to profit off US policy announcements by selling fast access to his social media posts
news.text:
APUS President Donald Trump holds up an image taken from his Truth Social account at an event about coal, in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington

NEW YORK - President Donald Trump knows the world hangs on his every word. Now he wants you to pay for it.The social media posts of the world's most powerful man are going on sale Saturday when his Truth Social business begins offering sneak peeks of them to Wall Street traders willing to pay up. The move raises the prospect of big profits for Trump's company and big questions about insider trading and using public office for private gain.Similar fast speed feeds are sold by other social media firms and media providers, but Truth Social doesn't just distribute the news, it makes it, regularly rattling markets as Trump posts policy changes on everything from war to central bank leadership to tariffs."If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time," said Irene Aldridge, head of Able Alpha Trading, which doesn't plan to buy the service. "We have a President of the United States who has the front seat to all the action, who makes all the decisions, and he's disclosing this ahead of time to a select group."Trump's company says critics just aren't capitalist enoughAsked about the propriety of the new service and whether White House lawyers had vetted it, Trump's press office declined to comment, referring questions to Truth Social's publicly traded parent. That company, Trump Media & Technology, issued a statement blasting Democratic critics for mischaracterizing the service "out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information - or, quite possibly, both."Live EventsA prolific poster, Trump has sent stocks, bonds and currencies soaring and plunging with his online musings and threats. That presents opportunities for so-called high frequency traders that specialize in buying and selling within milliseconds, exploiting tiny, fleeting difference in prices.Profits aplenty betting on oil, stocks and currenciesJust this month, Trump has threatened on Truth Social to slap higher tariffs on Canada, kill a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia and widen the Iran war. With advanced knowledge, traders betting on a plunge in the Canadian dollar, a drop in nuclear energy stocks and a jump in oil futures could have raked in big profits."For the big guys, it's going to be something they need," said Joe Saluzzi, co-founder of Themis Trading, who estimates about 100 of high frequency firms might be willing to pay for the service. "It's market-moving information."Dubbed Truth API, the service comes as these firms are spending more on feeds and servers that bypass slower internet connections with direct lines to news and data sources. The chance for profits is greater than ever thanks artificial intelligence's ability to read posts and articles more accurately for market-making changes and Trump's penchant for making news online.When Trump makes surprise announcements, traders pounceTraders profit when prices jump up and down, and with his taste for cliffhangers, threats and policy reversals America's first reality-TV president provides plenty of potentially market-moving content.The reversals are especially profitable, allowing traders to win both ways - jumping ahead of stocks moving up or down to a post threatening something, then cashing out within thousands of a second, then betting the other way.In addition to Trump, the service will include posts from other "high ranking" Truth Social contributors, including possibly his two oldest sons, Donald Jr. and Eric, who along with the father are heavily followed by users.Truth Social has said that the information will be released to the traders and the general public at the same time so there really isn't an issue of fairness. But Themis Trading's Saluzzi, a critic of high speed trading, says that's a red herring because when the posts are received, not when they are released, is what matters."Somebody who buys the info and has a system built to process it will be able to act quicker than you and me," said Saluzzi, adding in reference to everyday, small stock buyers, "The loser is always the retail investor."Trump posts about a company he likes, and stocks jumpAside from policy scoops, another reason to sign up has emerged in recent months: Trump is posting more about publicly traded companies, praising ones he likes in a way that sets off buying frenzies."The pimping of specific companies - obviously Wall Street would like to know that before other people," said Dylan Hedler-Gaudette, a federal ethics rule expert at the watchdog Project on Government Oversight. "It's a real mess."In April, moments after Trump praised Palantir Technologies in a post that included its stock symbol, the price briefly jumped the most it had in an entire year. Later that month, Trump posted, "Congratulations on Intel doing such a great job," and the stock immediately jumped in after-hours trading.Just which firms are signing up for the feed is unclear. Asked for comment, none of the half dozen most well known high-speed traders such as Citadel Securities and XTX Markets replied. If just three sign up for the $100,000 a month fee, that would double revenue at Trump Media, which reported taking in $3.7 million last year.Trump Media needs big money customersThe company can use their business.Stock in the Truth Social parent has plunged 75% since Trump took office last year as the company keeps reporting hundreds of millions in losses despite the president's help driving traffic to its site by posting major decisions there.In fact, the president breaks news on Truth Social so often that the White House press office will copy his posts into an email when responding to questions from the media seeking details on policies. If his posts aren't available yet, journalists are sometimes told, "Wait for the Truth."Another problem for Truth Social is looming if the Democrats take control of Congress and launch investigations, as vowed by Massachusetts Senator Sen. Elizabeth Warren in a statement Friday specifically attacking the new service: "We will haul in those responsible for this open corruption to answer to the American people."If the losses keep mounting for the company, though, some predict the president will push things further, using the platform even more for policy announcements."That's absolutely going to happen," warns Craig Holman, a lobbyist for the good government group Public Citizen. "Trump knows how to sell products."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: S.Y. Quraishi’s ‘India and I’: A civil servant’s journey through Indian history
news.text: In 1975, sometime after Indira Gandhi imposed Emergency, writer V.S. Naipaul found himself at a dinner gathering of bureaucrats in Chandigarh. Naipaul was travelling through India for what would become A Wounded Civilisation. During the evening, he struck up a conversation with a young civil servant whose story would eventually find its way into the book’s foreword. When Naipaul asked where he came from, the young man replied that his family had lived in Delhi for 500 years. “What in Europe would have sounded like boasting,” Naipaul wrote, “wasn’t boasting in India.” The young man traced his ancestry to Arabs who had settled in Delhi centuries earlier. He belonged to the generation of “midnight’s children”, born as India became independent after centuries of foreign rule—“Muslim for the first 500 years,” Naipaul wrote, “British for the last 150.” Coming from a modest family and becoming the first Muslim from Old Delhi to join IAS, he embodied, for Naipaul, the weight of history and the promise of a new India. “Indian history telescopes easily,” he noted. Half a century later, the young civil servant—S.Y. Quraishi, former chief election commissioner—returns to the same idea in India and I, a 100-chapter collection of reminiscences. The book shows that memory can indeed have a telescopic quality, compressing decades until distant events slide into one another. “Eighty years may be an entire lifetime for an individual, but it is only the opening chapter for a nation,” Quraishi writes. “When the republic shines, I feel proud. When it stumbles, I feel the bruise.” Organised into 11 thematic sections, the book doubles as both personal story and institutional history. What could have become a scattershot anthology of reminiscences is elevated into a coherent account by one of India’s most distinguished civil servants. The pages are populated by an eclectic cast: Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, Mohan Bhagwat and Javed Akhtar, and Alyque Padamsee and Hank Marvin. Like Marvin’s guitar, Quraishi—who played in a rock band at the IAS Academy with the delightfully quirky name Garibaldi and His Three Hairs—often makes memories reverberate. Perhaps, Quraishi has learnt something from Naipaul. “There was no notebook, no tape recorder, no obvious sign of an interview,” he writes about the conversation. “I had no inkling that Naipaul was storing it away.” Great writers are always working, he notes, and sometimes people become not just a source but a symbol—“a single thread Naipaul pulled to unravel something larger about the country he was trying to understand.” With India and I, Quraishi may well be inviting readers to pull a hundred such threads. EXCERPTS: The day I became an actor at FTII Tripurari Sharan, director of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), Pune, once invited me to speak at a conference on cinema and society in 2004. The theme intrigued me. At the time, I was deeply engaged in social welfare, especially women and child development, and one fact weighed on my mind: the scale of under-five mortality. Speaking about that before filmmakers, actors, and writers seemed both daunting and irresistible. The hall that morning was full of celebrities: Javed Akhtar, Shabana Azmi, Sudhir Mishra, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Saeed Mirza and several others. Each spoke about the power of cinema in awakening social conscience.When my turn came, I chose to speak about a story cinema rarely tells: around 6,000 under-five children dying each day, deaths that, in a more just world, should never occur. Midway through my speech, an idea came to me, risky, probably brash. Maybe it was the air of FTII, or maybe just my frustration at how numb we’d grown to grim statistics. I decided to play a prank, a small, dangerous experiment to make a big point. Pausing for effect, I reached into my pocket, took out my phone, and said in a grave voice: ‘Ladies and gentlemen, I’ve just received a message that there have been a series of explosions at Mumbai airport; thousands of people have died.’ The reaction was instantaneous. Faces went pale. People instinctively reached for their phones, searching for updates.Then I cut in quickly, before panic could spread. ‘I apologise. What I just said about explosions is not true. But what I am about to say is true: in the last twenty-four hours, around 6,000 under-five children have died, deaths that were entirely preventable.’ I ended the prank there. Mercifully, it was not the age of social media; otherwise, the rumour could have travelled faster than my clarification. But in that moment, I could see the impact. Relief, yes, but also something else. Discomfort, maybe embarrassment. ‘You see,’ I said, ‘you reacted instantly to just a mention of disaster. Yet the real catastrophe, six thousand young lives lost every day, barely moves you.’ Then I reached for a reference etched into public memory: Air India’s Kanishka, Flight 182, bombed on 23 June 1985. Three hundred and twenty-nine people died. We remember the number, the grief, the date. But if you translate under-five mortality into that arithmetic, the equivalent of roughly eighteen Kanishkas are crashing every single day, and we have somehow trained ourselves not to notice. The hall fell completely silent. The PMO posting I refused One day in the 1990s, my colleague Gupta walked into my office beaming. ‘Congratulations!’ he said. ‘You’ve been appointed joint secretary in the prime minister’s office.’ I was stunned. I knew nothing about it, and my first feeling was not of pride but alarm. I was joint secretary for youth affairs and director general of the Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, a network of 3,00,000 youth clubs across the country. I also headed the National Service Scheme in over three hundred universities. It was a rare posting where files did not imprison you. The work kept pulling me out into campuses, villages, small towns and remote districts. I loved it. The PMO was a dream posting for most officers: prestigious, powerful, close to the nerve centre. Yet for me, it raised three concerns. First, I did not want to leave a job that energised me. Second, I had silently decided to avoid three places, home, defence and the PMO, because, as a Muslim, I feared ‘extra vetting’. The idea offended me. I was an IAS officer, secular to the bone; I did not want my religion to become an additional file on someone’s table. Third, I was allergic to being a ‘representative’ slot. I wanted to be there as an officer, not a label. As soon as I reached home, I went to see my neighbour, N.K. Sinha, the additional secretary in the PMO who handled postings. He was visibly angry.‘How did you know?’ Once his irritation settled, I explained my reasons. He dismissed them. ‘There is no quota,’ he said. Then he added that minority matters sometimes benefited from a Muslim perspective. And finally, the truth: ‘You were selected directly by principal secretary A.N. Verma. You are the only name.’ I would not win on principle. So, I tried a different argument. Sinha was a devoted father. In the evenings, from our balcony, we could hear him teaching his two daughters maths, spelling or whatever the subject happened to be. My wife would tease me: ‘Look at him.What a good father!’ So, I said quietly, ‘Sir, my son and daughter are in classes 10 and 12 this year.’ He melted instantly. ‘Oh, I see! Suggest alternatives.’ Overnight, I studied the gradation list and prepared a note with about thirty officers and brief comments. After scanning it, he sighed. ‘Okay, okay.We’ll handle it.’ They did. The incumbent, Imtiaz Ahmad Khan, was given a two-year extension. Later, I met K.R. Venugopal, secretary to the prime minister. He listened, became serious, and said: ‘Yaqoob, you did the right thing. I had suggested your name earlier and was told, “We already have one Muslim.” You were being considered through that lens.’ My MoU that Donald Trump and Elon Musk questioned In 2012, I had exactly 13 days left as chief election commissioner when we signed an MoU with the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES), Washington, D.C. IFES, a non-government organisation, works in over 150 countries to strengthen democratic processes. It received funding from USAID, with whom India had excellent relations. I signed the MoU with its chairman, Bill Sweeney. The purpose was simple and unexceptionable. I had recently set up the IIIDEM (India International Institute of Democracy and Election Management). The idea was ambitious: besides training our 12 million election personnel, India would share its electoral experience with election managers from other countries, free of cost. Democracy was an export India could afford to give generously. The practical difficulty was obvious. We couldn’t have funded their travel and stay. Election officials would not travel to India merely to learn about Indian elections. They wanted training relevant to their own contexts. IFES agreed to bring international participants and provide expertise to customise programmes…. The MoU was professional and transparent. Crucially, it stated, twice, that there would be no legal or financial obligation on either side. In a five-page document, such a clause normally appears once. We included it twice. Uncanny, in hindsight. Years later, in 2025, after Donald Trump returned to the White House and Elon Musk headed a new Department of Government Efficiency, USAID funding to IFES came under attack and was stopped. news.title: Saudi crown prince urges Trump not to escalate Iran war: AP source
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom’s de facto leader, in a phone call with President Donald Trump on Saturday raised concerns about the U.S. potentially escalating the conflict with Iran, according to a person familiar with the leaders’ discussion.

The discussion, which was first reported on by Axios, comes as Trump weighs whether to carry out new strikes on Iran.

The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call but not authorized to comment publicly, are concerned that if the U.S. targets Iran’s energy infrastructure or carries out massive strikes on other key infrastructure that Tehran could respond by carrying out attacks on the kingdom’s and other Gulf countries’ energy infrastructure.

The crown prince during Saturday’s call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he’s weighing to take against Iran, the person said.

The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Saturday’s call.

Saudi Arabia earlier this week joined the U.S. in striking multiple logistics and weapons sites used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, but has been urging the U.S. and Iran to get back to the negotiating table to find an endgame to the five-month old conflict

The crown prince also dispatched his brother, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, to Washington earlier this week for separate meetings with Trump and Vice President JD Vance to discuss Iran strategy.

news.title: Vincent Pastore, who played 'Big Pussy' on 'The Sopranos,' dead at 80
news.text: Vincent Pastore, the actor best known for mob enforcer-turned-informant Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero on HBO's hit series "The Sopranos," has died at the age of 80, his manager told AFP on Saturday. Hollywood news outlet Deadline reported that the veteran actor, a native New Yorker, was found dead Saturday in his home in The Bronx. The manager, Robert Attermann, confirmed his death to AFP, but did not offer details about the circumstances. Born on July 14, 1946, Pastore served in the US Navy during the Vietnam War before earning a university degree in drama. He was often cast as a quintessential New York gangster, with film roles in Martin Scorsese's "Goodfellas" (1990) and Brian de Palma's "Carlito's Way" (1993). But his signature role was "Big Pussy," a right-hand man to Tony Soprano (the late James Gandolfini) who later became an FBI informant. His murder at the end of season two is one of the most iconic scenes in the Emmy-winning series' long run. "Not in the face, ok?" he says, before he is shot multiple times at point-blank range by Soprano and two other associates. He made guest appearances on many television series including "Law and Order" and "The Practice," and did voice acting in the animated "Shark Tale." He also appeared on several reality shows including "The Celebrity Apprentice," when Donald Trump was still hosting. "I had the privilege of representing Vinny for more than 30 years, long before 'The Sopranos' made him a household name," Attermann said in a statement. "To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable 'Big Pussy,' but to those of us who knew him, he was so much more," he said. "He loved being an actor. He was passionate about his craft and was always encouraging, respectful, and generous with young actors, taking the time to offer guidance and support whenever he could." bur-sst/acb

news.title: Brazil's Lula launches fourth term bid as Trump looms over campaign
news.text: At 80, President Lula on Sunday launches his bid for re-election, casting himself as a defender of Brazil's "sovereignty" as pressure from Donald Trump's administration casts a shadow over the campaign. Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a leftist titan of Latin American politics who is loved and despised in near-equal measure in Brazil, will launch his seventh bid for the presidency at a convention of his Worker's Party (PT) in Sao Paulo. The former metalworker and unionist made a dramatic comeback when he returned to power three years ago after a stint in jail on corruption charges that were later dismissed, and two previous terms from 2003-2010. He is seeking a fourth term in office in a race that carries a strong sense of deja vu in the polarized nation where the past two elections pitted a PT candidate against far-right firebrand Jair Bolsonaro. This time Lula's main rival is the former president's eldest son Flavio Bolsonaro. The 45-year-old senator stepped into the role after his father was convicted of plotting a coup to prevent Lula from taking power in 2023. The Bolsonaro family is allied with US President Donald Trump, who has backed several victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America and whose shadow looms large over the Brazilian campaign. "In Brazil, we do not accept anyone sticking their nose where it does not belong," said Lula. In July, the United States imposed two rounds of tariffs on Brazilian goods, alleging unfair trade practices which Brasilia denies. Last year, encouraged by another of Jair Bolsonaro's sons, Eduardo, Washington hiked tariffs in retaliation for the trial against the former leader. These were largely lifted after diplomatic efforts. Staring down a renewed trade war, Lula has built his strategy around defending Brazilian sovereignty and reminding voters of his four decades as the country's most consequential political figure. He has derided Flavio Bolsonaro as a "traitor to the nation." "The sovereignty message comes at the perfect time for Lula. At a moment when he was experiencing a drop in popularity it allows him to identify an external enemy to blame for some of the problems we are facing," Leonardo Paz, a political science professor at the Getulio Vargas Foundation, told AFP. - Crime and corruption - Flavio Bolsonaro is promising change: he wants to 'free' Brazil of crime, inflation, high taxes, and Lula, who is seeking a fourth term in office (768x511, AR: 1.50)A recent survey by the Datafolha institute showed that 48 percent of those polled would vote for Lula in a second round. Flavio scored 43 percent despite being battered by a series of scandals. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin. The veteran leftist's administration boasts solid economic growth and record employment levels. But families complain about the cost of living and the fiscal deficit is worsening. The incumbent is also on the back foot when it comes to Brazilians' top concern: security. Tens of millions of people live in poor neighborhoods controlled by organized crime. Corruption allegations have touched both campaigns. Flavio Bolsonaro is under scrutiny for seeking money from a banker accused of major financial fraud to fund a film about his father. news.title: Capital One responds to stoush with Trump Organization
news.text: Capital One Financial has hit back against a lawsuit over its decision to close the ‌Trump Organization's bank accounts years ago, stating that it did so after a review by anti-money laundering experts. The disclosure marks the first time ‌a bank has formally tied money laundering concerns to US President Donald Trump's family business. Capital One is seeking to dismiss the case by casting doubt on claims of illegally debanking - or denying services on religious or political grounds - the Trump Organization. Capital One has never accused the Trump Organization of illegal money laundering. But Friday's filing argues ‌that "documents and Plaintiffs' ‌own allegations make ⁠clear that Capital One closed Plaintiffs' accounts for anti-money laundering ("AML") reasons. The closures were the result ​of months of analysis and a careful review by Capital One's AML team in accordance with bank policies and regulatory guidance." Capital One gave notice of its plans to close more than 300 Trump-affiliated bank accounts in March 2021. The Trump Organization and Eric Trump, the president's son, filed a lawsuit in March 2025 in a Florida federal court, alleging the accounts were closed because of Capital One's "woke" beliefs and its desire ⁠to benefit from the political mood after the January 6, 2021 riot ‌at the ​US Capitol. The federal court in Miami has tossed two complaints in the Capital One case, but gave the ​plaintiffs opportunities each time ‌to submit an amended complaint. Capital One said that the latest version, filed in July, "suffers from the same fundamental flaws as ​their prior two pleadings". Capital One said in Friday's filing that the Trump Organization's allegations of political pretext were "misguided" and "based on cherry-picked quotations unsupported by the full context" of documents submitted to the court. "The transaction patterns identified by Capital One are among ​the ​types of activity flagged by federal banking guidance," the filing ​said. Since the start of Trump's second term, his administration has put ‌pressure on some large banks, echoing conservative complaints that the institutions are deliberately targeting the political right. Trump signed an executive order in August 2025 barring discriminatory debanking. In January, Trump filed a suit against JPMorgan Chase on the same grounds, underscoring the fraught policy environment Wall Street is navigating during the president's second term. In 2019, during his first term, Trump sued Capital One and Deutsche Bank in an attempt ​to prevent them from sharing financial records with Congress as part of a probe led by Democratic lawmakers. Anti-money laundering professionals ​at Deutsche Bank reportedly flagged a set ⁠of transactions, but executives ignored them; Deutsche Bank denied the report at the time. Australian Associated Press

news.title: Trump slams prosecutor over Reflecting Pool case withdrawal
news.text:
US president Donald Trump criticised his hand-picked prosecutor for dropping charges against a former Olympian arrested amid the Reflecting Pool controversy. (EPA Images pic)
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump's extraordinary campaign to blame an apparently botched renovation of Washington's Reflecting Pool on vandals took another twist Saturday when he attacked his hand-picked prosecutor for dropping charges against an ex-Olympian arrested in the controversy.
Trump lashed out at federal prosecutor Jeanine Pirro - a former Fox News host who has been a longtime supporter of the Republican president - after she sought to dismiss the charges, acknowledging in court documents that poor installation, not vandalism, apparently wrecked the multimillion-dollar renovation on the National Mall.
"I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the US Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool. I don't know what she was thinking?" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM."
Trump then appeared to tacitly acknowledge what had long been suspected by politicians and the press: that a botched and hurried process had led a new "American Flag blue" sealant to both peel from the pool's bottom and promote rapid algae growth.
"There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!" Trump said.
He also shared security camera footage he claimed showed vandalism.
In the video individuals are seen from afar putting their hands into the water while workers undertook cleaning work, but it did not clearly show people damaging the pool or depositing anything into it.
Trump is spending the weekend at his New Jersey golf club outside New York City.
The attack on his long-time ally came amid other posts of a war plane, gold-plated statues and what appeared to be a campaign poster of himself running for a third term, which would be illegal under the US Constitution.
Trump had made the renovation a national drama by repeatedly discussing plans and providing regular updates of the expedited work ahead of America's 250th anniversary celebrations earlier this summer.
When the pool liner began peeling off and algae grew quickly despite the application of chemicals, Trump blamed vandalism for the damage while providing no meaningful evidence.
Former Olympian David Hearn, 67, was arrested and charged with felony vandalism, which could have seen him jailed for a decade. He pleaded not guilty.
On Friday, Pirro filed documents seeking dismissal of the case, saying new revelations "undermine the evidentiary basis for the indictment."
She said new documents indicate that damage to the landmark was "the result of flawed installation by the contractor... and the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration."
A Trump cabinet member, interior secretary Doug Burgum, repeated the president's talking points Saturday.
"The evidence is clear, vandals have repeatedly caused damage to the Reflecting Pool," Burgum posted on X. "We won't back down to deranged people who want to destroy, deface, or degrade our monuments."
news.summary: Court documents say that poor installation, not vandalism, wrecked the multimillion-dollar renovation on the National Mall.

news.title: World News | Top US General Warns Pentagon He Lacks Enough Naval Forces to Protect Israel from Iranian Attacks: Report
news.text:
Washington, DC [US], August 2 (ANI): A top American military commander stationed in Europe has cautioned the Pentagon that Washington may soon confront hard decisions on missile defence resources as the ongoing conflict with Iran continues to place heavy pressure on American military stockpiles.

The development was reported by The Washington Post, which noted that the chief of US European Command, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, informed Pentagon officials earlier this week that the United States lacks adequate naval assets to continue intercepting Iranian ballistic missile strikes on Israel.
